Witch killings

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How in 2018 are woman being assaulted and murdered for being suspected witches

Summary:
When a video of two woman being violently assaulted went viral recently it again brought up how vulnerable woman are in communities that believe in witches.
These two woman in the video were first robbed, stripped of their clothes and assaulted. They then ran into the village in Grabowe looking for help and were attacked by the community, as the community members thought they were witches that had flown into the village to curse them. This sounds far fetched, but according to the HRC in the Eastern Cape this is a common belief that is leading to so many woman being persecuted. In many communities through out SA people believe that witches are skinny, dark woman who live alone and these woman are often persecuted when something goes wrong in the community.
This case is just one, but we have other case studies from the East Cape where woman have been murdered. One old lady was burnt in her house last year, in front of her grandchild, because it was believed she was a witch

Prof Juan Nel has put together a study on hate crimes in SA and specifically on the persecution of witches, he has statistics and a lot of very interesting sociological information on understanding why this happens

The question is, if this is so prevalent why are we not having sensitisation campaigns about it? Where is the education that can change the way people think about these woman?

Just because these woman are in largely rural areas does not mean they do not deserve to be protected.



Further information:
CASE STUDIES:
The two woman in the video who were assaulted
The family of a woman who was murdered in the Eastern Cape
One of the Villagers from Grabowe - I think it would be good to hear it from the horses mouth. This fear the community have of witches.

Experts
Prof Juan
Kerry from the Commission for Gender Equality is going to connect me with a person of colour from the HRC or the CGE who can speak on the issue at large

Then who do we confront about why these people aren't being protected?


Case Study:
Petrus Majola

Expert:
Mr. Prof Juan Nel
Miss. Kerry

Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:00 Nobekho Mandiyane When I arrived, they said “here is another witch! Why are you dressed? “and they took off my clothes
2 00:12 Agnes Mondiane They said my house is burnt, they told me what happened and I started crying.
3 00:18 Clair Link When I say which hunts you immediately think of fairy tales or women being burnt at the stake 100 of years ago but in fact right now in 2018 people being accused as witches are being persecuted all over south Africa.
4 00:34 Claire voice over Agnus is from a township near Mpumalanga, where there is a strong belief in witchcraft. In February Agnus was suffering from a mental breakdown and
started acting out of character; the community viewed this behaviour as a sign
that she was a witch.
5 00:49 Agnes I was found in church and I wasn’t wearing shoes, they said that I hadn’t combed my hair, I hadn’t showered, and I want even wearing a bra. They said I entered the church and swore at the congregation
6 01:02 Voice over After her behaviour in the church the community violently attacked Agnus for being a witch
7 01:07 Video of Agnes being beaten

8 01:12 Voice over It’s hard to believe the women in the viral video is the Agnes I met.
9 01:17 Agnes I could feel that these people are hitting me, but I don’t understand what was going on. When I saw the video of myself I went home and I couldn’t sleep, I felt pain. I asked this lady “is this how they were pulling me”? they were pulling me by my feet all over
10 01:38 Voice over Nobekho was living in a township near Grabouw, when she was accused of
being a witch. It all started when her Friend was caught naked by a neighbour,
because of her nudity she was branded a witch who had fallen from her
broom
11 01:52 Claire link Afraid, she tried to save herself and admitted that she and Nobukho were witches
12 01:59 Voice over the angry mob ripped Nobekho from her home in the early hours of the morning
13 02:02 Nobekho There were a lot of men and they were carrying sticks and they said “let’s go”. When I arrived, their people said “here is the other witch”. “witch, take off those clothes” then I said “I’m not a witch”. They took off my clothes. They beat us in the rain and it was cold. They beat us with sjamboks, they were beating us and even people on their wat to work in the morning joined in on the beating.
14 02:27 Voice over Agnus and Nobekho stories are not unique. Witch-hunts have been taking place, largely in rural areas, for year where there is a strong culture belief in the power of witches to do evil.
Dr. Yaseen Ally is a research psychologist at Nelson Mandela University and has been researching supernatural beliefs for 10 years.
15 02:48 Claire and Dr Yaseen Dr Yaseen: the belief in witch craft is a real experience for many people and because that experience of the belief is witches are considered to be real. Obviously, there is a lot of fear attached to it and that’s what motivates people wanting to be violent towards the witch fear.
Claire: so, people are genuinely afraid of witches?
Dr. Yaseen: absolute and it boils down to the fear, and the belief of what witch craft is capable of doing.
16 03:12 Voice over This fear means a woman can be senselessly accused of being a witch simply for the way she looks or because the community is jealous
Ms Nomisi Bata is the commissioner at the Commission for gender quality explains further
16 03:25 Claire and Nomsisi interview Claire: People when they hear about witches and witch hunts they dismiss it and they think it’s not part of their belief system, so where does this belief come from?
Nomsisi: You would live in a village or in a township and you would be successful. Some people are easily labeled as using witch craft to get to the success. Also, this thing of people dying in the village, people die because they are sick but because people go and try and find out from traditional healers who is responsible for my child’s death. Then because the sniffing points it to me they say it’s her who has bewitched my child.
Claire: and for people who don’t know what sniffing is, could you explain what it is?
Nomsisi: in isiXhosa, they say Uyonukisa (sniffing) you smell the person.
Claire: is a traditional healer figuring out who did this?
Nomsisi: yeah

17 04:24 Voice over A traditional healer is seen as someone who uses their power for good, while people believe that a witch is someone who uses their power for evil.
18 04:33 Claire and Dr Yaseen Dr. Yaseen: one of the means of making sense of this is the reliance on the theory of misfortune because that is what witch craft basically represents. It’s the theory of misfortune that helps people represent the bad things that are happening in their life
19 04:47 Voice over A community suffering from poverty, unemployment or illness is more likely to turn to this belief in witchcraft to make sense of their own misfortune. Jealously may have been a motivation for the attack on Agnus, as she had just built her family a three-bedroom home, which the community set on fire.
Everything she had worked so hard to achieve, everything she owned was burnt to the ground
20 05:15 Agnes I had built a home and I thought I was done. I was hurt and the thing that hurt me the most is that this thing happened to me on my birthday, the 6th of February. Then always when the 6th of February comes I pray to God… asking him to change this day because the day it took place was on my birthday. So, I don’t know why it happened on my birthday, that’s the thing.
21 05:56 Dr Yaseen and Claire interview Dr. Yaseen: the means of actually purging a community from someone accused of witch craft is extreme violence.
Claire: with the intention to kill?
Dr. Yasseen: and the reason for this is the belief in witch craft leaves community members to the understanding that unless they eradicate this threat they will not be safe.
22 06:13 Nobekho They beat us and then they asked for petrol so they can burn the witches. I was worried because I knew I was going to die because a person from Siyanyanzela is beaten until they die. The way they were beating me I knew I was dying
23 06:31 Claire and Dr. Yaseen Claire: How many women are being victimised? Do you have an estimate?
Dr. Yaseen: It’s very difficult for me to estimate, some years it can go up to 150 women in other years it drops down to maybe 20.
24 06:41 Voice over No-one in these communities would speak to us; everyone was adamant that they don’t believe in witches.
25 06:47 Claire Claire: Why are we not hearing about this witch hunt other than a viral video popping up once in a while?
Dr. Yaseen: its fear, people are so afraid of witch craft that they are afraid to talk about it and one of the reasons for that is the belief is that witches can actually listen in on these conversations when they’re being spoken about. And they would then come for you and attack you
26 07:08 Nomsisi and Claire Nomsisi: Even with the SAPS those crimes statistics are not desegregated to be able to pick up that these particular murders are witch craft murders. They should be branded as such
Claire: are these witch or people being accused of being witches mostly women?
Nomsisi: They are women, 99% of them are women. This is another form of gender based violence? Why is witchcraft having the face of a women? Its bias towards branding women as witches. Predominantly traditional healers are men but when it comes to people who are bewitching people its women.
07:53 Voice over Even though it is woman being persecuted, the perpetrators are not only men, and the whole community takes part in this mob violence. Once an accusation of witchcraft has been laid the mob is the judge, juror and executioner.
28 08:08 Nobekho The paramedics took me to the emergency ward and when I came to I saw the friend who was being beaten with me, and I asked “why did you accuse me of witchcraft”? and she said “I wanted them to leave us alone” and I kept quiet and then left her alone
29 08:24 Claire and Dr. Yaseen Claire: so how safe are women in rural areas from being accused or falsely accused of being witches?
Dr. Yaseen: the moment an accusation of witch craft is levelled at a woman there is no safety. If a woman is able to survive the witchcraft accusation and the violence, she would be facing with complete abandonment and isolation. In fact, most of these women would have to leave their communities of the fear of being killed.
30 08:49 Voice over Nobekho was forced to move back to her village in the Eastern cape with
her daughter, while her husband stayed in Grabouw for work. Their family has been torn apart
31 09:00 Nobekho I will never go back to Grabouw, I will stay here in the village because I can’t of through what I went through again or I will die. I will not go back to Grabouw. I will stay here in the village.

32 9:21 Voice over Agnus was left homeless and forced to move into this one bedroom back room with her three children, far away from her family and the people she once called friends.
33 09:32 Agnes I was scared to even go to the shop, I was scared to even walk outside. I used to stay inside the house. My life hasn’t been okay, I was confused a lot because the people that did this to me it was the people whom I didn’t expect. The people that beat me are the same, I didn’t expect that they would do that. the same people who had videos of me are the same people I was close to.
